title: Creatine kinase
subtitle: Muscle injury, rhabdomyolysis and renal-risk features
summary: Muscle injury, rhabdomyolysis and renal-risk features
introduction: Interpret CK against the laboratory upper limit, muscle mass, exercise, trauma, seizure, medication and renal function. CK can continue rising for hours after injury; repeat testing may be necessary.

rows.name: Raised CK
rows.referenceRange: RVH adult CK reference: male 39–308 U/L; female 26–192 U/L. Retain clinical rhabdomyolysis thresholds separately.
notes: Causes include prolonged immobilisation, crush injury, seizure, hyperthermia, extreme exercise, ischaemia, infection, inflammatory myopathy, statins or toxins. Risk depends on CK trend, creatinine, potassium, phosphate, calcium, hydration and urine output.

rows.name: Marked elevation
rows.referenceRange: CK >5,000 U/L often indicates higher AKI risk
notes: This is not an absolute treatment threshold. AKI and dangerous hyperkalaemia can occur at lower values, particularly with dehydration, sepsis or baseline renal disease.

urgentFindings: Dark urine, oliguria, severe muscle pain/swelling, profound weakness or compartment-type pain.
Raised CK with potassium elevation, creatinine rise, metabolic acidosis or ECG changes.
Hyperthermia, prolonged seizure, crush injury or prolonged immobilisation with systemic illness.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: Long-lie / immobility rhabdomyolysis
findings: History of a long lie, fall with inability to get up, or prolonged immobilisation
interpretation: Prolonged pressure on muscle causes breakdown and releases CK, potassium and myoglobin; this is easy to miss if a long lie is not specifically asked about, particularly in older adults found on the floor
actions: Actively ask about time spent on the floor/immobile, and examine for pressure areas and compartment-type pain
Request U&E to check potassium and renal function alongside CK (see further testing)
Encourage oral fluids where safe, and treat as time-critical if there is hyperkalaemia, AKI or systemic illness (see urgent findings)

commonPatterns.title: Exertional rhabdomyolysis
findings: Recent extreme or unaccustomed exercise, heat exposure, or exercising while unwell
interpretation: Strenuous exercise, particularly in heat or in an unaccustomed or unfit individual, can cause significant muscle breakdown even without trauma or a long lie
actions: Ask specifically about recent exercise intensity, hydration during exercise and any heat exposure
Encourage oral rehydration where safe and appropriate, and request U&E to assess renal function and potassium (see further testing)
Treat as time-critical if there are features of AKI, hyperkalaemia or systemic illness (see urgent findings)

commonPatterns.title: Seizure or crush-injury rhabdomyolysis
findings: Recent prolonged or repeated seizure activity, or a crush/entrapment injury
interpretation: Sustained muscle contraction (prolonged seizure) or direct muscle injury (crush) can cause severe rhabdomyolysis, sometimes with a delayed peak in CK after the initial event
actions: Establish the duration of seizure activity or the mechanism and duration of crush/entrapment
Request U&E and consider repeat CK, as levels can continue rising for hours after the injury (see further testing)
Treat as time-critical if there is dark urine, oliguria, hyperkalaemia or ECG change (see urgent findings)

commonPatterns.title: Medication/statin-related CK rise
findings: CK raised, often mild to moderate
Current statin or other myotoxic medication, without a clear alternative precipitant
interpretation: Statins and some other medicines can cause a myopathy with raised CK ranging from asymptomatic elevation to severe rhabdomyolysis; muscle pain and weakness support a clinically significant reaction rather than an incidental finding
actions: Ask specifically about muscle pain, weakness and timing relative to starting or increasing the medication
Review the medication list for other interacting or myotoxic drugs
Arrange medical review for consideration of stopping/changing the medication if the rise is significant or symptomatic; treat as time-critical if severe (see urgent findings)

commonPatterns.title: Isolated mild CK rise, low apparent risk
findings: No long lie, crush injury, seizure, extreme exertion or significant medication history
interpretation: A mild rise without a clear precipitant and without renal, potassium or systemic derangement is lower risk, but the absence of a precipitant should still be actively checked for rather than assumed
5,000 U/L is a commonly cited marker of higher AKI risk, but AKI and dangerous hyperkalaemia can occur at lower levels, particularly with dehydration or baseline renal disease
actions: Confirm renal function and potassium are normal before treating the result as reassuring (see further testing)
Safety-net for dark urine, reduced urine output or worsening symptoms, and arrange repeat CK if the trend is unclear
Reassess if any precipitant (long lie, exertion, medication, seizure) is subsequently identified

rationale: Assesses renal function and potassium, which drive the acute risk from rhabdomyolysis more than the CK level alone
Deranged calcium and phosphate are relevant in significant rhabdomyolysis and should be checked alongside U&E
Gives a rapid assessment of acidosis and lactate, which support severity assessment in significant rhabdomyolysis
A dipstick strongly positive for blood without red cells on microscopy supports myoglobinuria and is a quick bedside clue to significant muscle breakdown
CK can continue rising for hours after the precipitating injury, so a single early result may underestimate the peak — repeat testing helps confirm the trend
Identifies ECG changes of hyperkalaemia, which is a key time-critical complication of significant rhabdomyolysis

specimens.notes: Plasma — green-top lithium-heparin tube with yellow insert, 3 mL.
